flags: minor: distractors are weak; B and C are absolute claims the passage directly contradicts (P5 'none of this proves... only reason'; P4 uses the correlation as a starting point), and A is the hypothesis P2 undercuts, so the item is close to a gimme
R035-01.notes: The passage weighs rival explanations and ends saying the fly hypothesis has experimental support the others lack. A is undercut in P2, B contradicts P5, C is too extreme.

R035-02.notes: The sentence sets up the rest of the passage, which covers studies able to tell the explanations apart. B overstates ('disproved'), C has no support, and D is wrong because the fly idea is not presented as new to earlier biologists.

R035-03.notes: 'Took that reply seriously' means the study tested the defenders' claim about predator vision. A is the opposite of the finding, C reverses it, and D is wrong because the study used vision, not hearing or smell.

R035-04.notes: Even within the range where a lion can resolve the stripes, it would already have detected the zebra another way, so the stripes add little concealment. D is a plausible trap because it mixes up who detects whom, and A overgeneralizes with 'every'.

flags: minor: the key closely paraphrases the first sentence of P4 ('Correlation, though, could not show that the stripes did anything'), so the item is close to a lookup
minor: C and D directly contradict P3 ('dozens of environmental factors'; 'not with predators')
R035-05.notes: It was a correlational analysis that linked striping to fly-active regions but did not show that the stripes have any effect.

flags: minor: possible overlap with R035-07, since both rest on the same P4 contrast between approaching and landing
R035-06.notes: Flies circled both animals equally, so they found the zebras, but they landed less often, so their landings were disrupted. A is contradicted by the equal circling. C ignores the drop in landings.

flags: minor: the key's wording ('the fewer landings came from the coats' pattern, not the horses') is a little awkward and may cost some students a moment
R035-07.notes: The uncovered heads act as a control: the same horses drew equal landings on their heads, so the drop on their bodies comes from the coat pattern and not from the horses themselves. B and C are unsupported, and C contradicts the head data.

R035-08.notes: 'Each idea has had its champions' means each idea has had supporters. A, the everyday 'winners' sense, is the only real trap.

R035-09.notes: D reverses the stripe–fly association from the 2014 analysis. A bears on camouflage, not on flies. B is compatible with the fly hypothesis because P5 says a trait can serve more than one purpose. C changes little, since circling was never the mechanism and slightly more circling with fewer landings still fits the hypothesis. B and C are reasonable traps.

passage_flags: minor: the 2014 analysis (Caro et al., Nature Communications) tested a limited set of variables for each hypothesis; 'dozens of environmental factors' may overstate it. R035-05 choice D depends on this wording but is wrong either way.

Other study details match the published work as far as I know: Melin et al. 2016 (lions resolve stripes at about 50 m in daylight, less at dusk) and Caro et al. 2019 (Somerset, UK farm; similar approach rates but fewer landings on zebras; flies failing to slow down; black, white and striped horse coats; equal landings on uncovered heads).
